{
  "need": "Autonomy",
  "secondary": { "name": "Identity" },
  "read": "A new hire walking in Monday has no track record here yet, which means their status is essentially zero — they know nothing about how things work, who trusts them, or whether they even belong. The biggest risk is that a one-way expectations download lands as 'you are the least important person in the room,' triggering either quiet withdrawal or early friction. The identity piece shows up because they are still figuring out what kind of professional they are becoming, and your first conversation will shape that story.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Enforcer", "instinct": "Lay out every rule and consequence up front so there are no surprises — but that signals surveillance over trust and makes them feel like a problem you are already bracing for." },
  "mentorMove": "Open with genuine curiosity about what they want to build, then tie your standards to their goals rather than your authority — so the expectations feel like tools for their success, not fences around your comfort.",
  "holdFirm": ["The standards themselves — quality of work, reliability, communication norms, and how mistakes get handled — are not up for negotiation.", "The timeline and accountability structure stays intact even as you give them room to find their own rhythm inside it."],
  "stayFlexible": ["How they prefer to check in, ask questions, or flag problems can flex around their style.", "The order in which they ramp up on responsibilities can be shaped by what they bring to the table and what they want to tackle first."],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 3, "label": "Collaboration" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, welcome — really glad you are here. Before we get into logistics I want to take ten minutes to hear from you. What made you want this role, and what do you actually want to get out of the next year or so?" },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "That is helpful context. What do you think is going to be the trickiest part of the job for you to get comfortable with? I am asking because I have found that the earlier we name the hard stuff, the less it catches us off guard." },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Here is what I care most about on this team: we deliver good work on time, we communicate early when something is off track, and we treat each other like adults who can handle honest feedback. I want to build that with you, not just hand you a rulebook. So let me share where the firm lines are, and then I want to hear what kind of support actually helps you do your best work." },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I hold everyone here to a high bar because I think you are all capable of it — and that includes you, starting day one. I am not going to lower the standard because you are new; what I am going to do is stay close so you have what you need to meet it. I am genuinely confident you can, otherwise we would not have made this offer. Let us check in at the end of each of your first four weeks and adjust from there — does that work for you?" }
  ],
  "longGame": "The way you run Monday sets the psychological contract for the whole relationship — if they leave that first conversation feeling seen and trusted rather than warned and watched, they will bring you problems early instead of hiding them, and that is the single biggest predictor of how well a new hire performs in the first six months."
}
situation: A new hire starts Monday and I want to set clear expectations.
